title: The oldest question
hookLine: the voices this year listens to each speak about death, and they do not agree

lines: A CHILD ASKS WITH THE LIGHT OFF.
cards: What happens when we die? A child asks it at bedtime, out of nowhere, with the light already off. An adult asks it at a funeral, quietly, or not at all.
Call it the oldest question, though nobody can put a date on that. The voices this year listens to each have something to say about death, and they don't say the same thing.
A new block begins, and before anyone else speaks, one voice goes first: yours.

teach.b: First, they don't agree. In the weeks ahead, Socrates will offer two possibilities and refuse to pick. An Epicurean poet will say death is nothing to us.
Buddhists will speak of rebirth without a fixed soul passing on. The Gita will speak of a self that sets down bodies like worn clothes.
Christians will speak of resurrection, Muslims of a day when every deed is weighed, Confucius of attending to life first.
These aren't one answer in different costumes, and this block keeps each in its own home, as the block on suffering did. Second, the Bible has a book that sits squarely in this question.

teach.h: A TIME TO BE BORN, A TIME TO DIE.
teach.b: Ecclesiastes says there is "a time to be born, and a time to die." It doesn't explain the second half. It sets the two side by side.
Third, why start with you. Across weeks of teachers, it's easy to lose track of what you thought before they spoke.

teach.h: WRITE WHAT YOU THINK BEFORE THEY SPEAK.
teach.b: So today you write it down plainly, in a few lines: what you think happens, what you hope, what you fear, and what you honestly don't know. At the end of the block, you'll be invited to write it again and see what moved.
Fourth, gently. Death is not an abstract topic for anyone grieving.

teach.h: GENTLY, IF THE LOSS IS FRESH.
teach.b: If a loss is fresh, it's fine to go slowly through these weeks, or to sit a practice out.
The question has waited a long time. It can wait for you.

how: Some people exploring death across traditions begin by writing down what they believe now, so they can notice later what the teachers changed and what they didn't.

games.q: a block of teachers on death is about to begin. what do you do first?
o: wait to hear them all before thinking anything.
write what you think now, in a few plain lines.
pick the teacher who sounds most comforting.
games.why: your voice goes first. writing it down now lets you see later what moved and what didn't.

practice: Ask yourself plainly: what do I think happens when we die?
It may be the answer you were raised with or one you came to on your own; notice what comes first, a picture, a word, a shrug, a fear, a face, or I don't know, which is an answer too.
Let it come and stay, as plain as a grocery list.

carryVoice: Your line: what I think now. A few plain lines, dated, waiting for the end of the block. That's day seven hundred fifty-nine.
